title: webtools-http common core
issueTitle: webtools-http: module skeleton, opt-in marker, failure model, request/response types, transport and wall-clock ports, logging seam and the check-only `js` compile
function: WebTools has no HTTP stack of its own: `Connector`, a blocking line reader over `URLConnection`, is its only HTTP client, and nothing offers a suspend request, a typed failure model or a transport port (#55 architecture §2). This run creates the `webtools-http` module and its check-only `js` sibling `webtools-http-commoncheck`, and delivers the vocabulary every later unit of #55 speaks: the opt-in marker, the failure model with its two reason vocabularies, the request and response types, the transport and wall-clock ports and the logging seam. Unit 3 of #55: one new module's additive API inside one system; every default implementation and policy is left to the units after it.

gap.summary: No `webtools-http` module exists. The build includes the three existing modules only, and the multiplatform convention that #61 shipped is applied by no module yet, so nothing in the repository offers a suspend request, a typed failure model or a transport port.
evidence: settings.gradle.kts:11 — `include(":webtools-udp", ":webtools-scraping", ":webtools-browser")` (baseline)
build-logic/src/main/kotlin/webtools.kotlin-multiplatform-library.gradle.kts:7 — the convention for a published multiplatform library with a single `jvm()` target; no module applies it (baseline)

options.name: A Kotlin Multiplatform module on `webtools.kotlin-multiplatform-library`, `jvm()` only, with `explicitApi()`, the ABI dump and `kotlinx-coroutines-core` 1.10.2 as its one `api` dependency
options.why: OkHttp, Caffeine and slf4j stay `implementation` in `jvmMain`, so no implementation library reaches a consumer's compile classpath. Coroutines is `api` because it is the runtime of a suspend API and `CoroutineDispatcher` appears in configuration, which lets one virtual clock drive the cache, the budget and `delay`.

options.name: An `.internal` subpackage beside the public one
options.why: `internal` already does the hiding, and one flat package `com.spartanlabs.webtools.http` never needs a type to move.

options.name: An opaque library-owned `Scheduling` value in place of `CoroutineDispatcher` in configuration, keeping coroutines `implementation`
options.why: A consumer could no longer pass its own dispatcher, such as a `limitedParallelism` view that bounds parse threads; every component would gain a bespoke type in place of the idiom, and it would keep off the compile classpath nothing a suspend API's consumer does not already have.

options.name: KGP's built-in `abiValidation` instead of binary-compatibility-validator for the ABI dump
options.why: It is experimental on Kotlin 2.2.0, and its DSL changed by 2.4.

options.name: Adding `kotlinx-coroutines-test` to the module's tests
options.why: No test of this unit needs it: `runBlocking` in `jvmTest` covers the non-fatal helper. Unit 4 adds it on its fixtures variant.

gap.summary: No opt-in gate exists for the seams a consumer implements. The stack's rule puts every such seam behind one `@RequiresOptIn` marker while the supplied defaults stay usable without opting in, and the repository has no marker of its own.
evidence: ../research/README.md § The work, Stability — every seam a consumer implements or substitutes sits behind one marker; the defaults need no opt-in

options.name: One marker at level `ERROR` with an empty `@Target`, applied only through `@SubclassOptInRequired`
options.why: `@SubclassOptInRequired` is stable on Kotlin 2.2.0 and gates implementing and delegating but not mentioning a type, so constructing and calling the supplied defaults needs no opt-in. With an empty target the marker can only be the argument of `@SubclassOptInRequired` and `@OptIn`. It is never removed, even after every seam graduates to `@SupportedExtension`.

options.name: The marker placed directly on the seam types
options.why: A directly marked type in a default-path signature contaminates every caller; placed only through `@SubclassOptInRequired`, a default-path signature can never force the opt-in on a caller.

options.name: The opt-in as `kotlin { compilerOptions { optIn.add(...) } }`, as a target-level option, or through `sourceSets.all { }`
options.why: Each of them also reaches `commonTest` and `jvmTest`, which would then compile as a non-consumer and could implement a port or subclass a failure group without the `@OptIn` a consumer needs.
options.source: plan.md R7, §6.2; research/opt-in-gate.md F2, F3, F5

options.name: The opt-in set in a convention plugin
options.why: A module that cannot see the marker would print an unresolved-marker warning on every compile; the language setting belongs to the main source sets of each module's own build file.

verdict.summary: One marker, `ExperimentalForInheritanceWebToolsApi`: `@RequiresOptIn(level = ERROR)` with its message as one string literal, an empty `@Target`, `BINARY` retention, used only through `@SubclassOptInRequired` and `@OptIn`, never removed. The main source sets opt in as a language setting of `commonMain` and `jvmMain` in the module's own build file, and the check module's of `commonMain` and `jsMain`; the test source sets stay without it.

rows.name: The failure model and its two reason vocabularies
rows.where: common/ — HttpFailure, TransportFailure, UpstreamFailure, RefusalReason, ExhaustedReason

gap.summary: No typed HTTP failure exists, and nothing carries one in `Result`. The repository's precedent is `webtools-udp`'s open `ReliableSendFailure`, carried in `Result` and deliberately not sealed; its `Result.flatMap` helper is `internal` and copied per module on purpose.
evidence: webtools-udp/src/main/kotlin/com/spartanlabs/webtools/udp/ReliableSendFailure.kt:15 — `abstract class ReliableSendFailure(message: String) : Exception(message)` (baseline)
webtools-udp/src/main/kotlin/com/spartanlabs/webtools/udp/ResultExtensions.kt:3-5 — the internal `flatMap`, deliberately duplicated in `webtools-scraping` (baseline)

options.name: An open, subclass-gated `abstract class HttpFailure : Exception` in `kotlin.Result`: the groups `TransportFailure` and `UpstreamFailure`, final leaves, one shared `Closed`, and the open constants classes `RefusalReason` and `ExhaustedReason`
options.why: It follows `ReliableSendFailure`: a leaf or a reason may be added in a feature release, and the KDoc says to match the groups and keep an `else`. Messages carry a constant per type and non-sensitive fields only. Cancellation is thrown, never wrapped: an internal non-fatal catch helper converts only exceptions other than `CancellationException`, and no `runCatching` wraps a suspend call.

options.name: A sealed failure root, or enums for the library-produced reasons
options.why: Each added leaf or entry is a compile error in a consumer's exhaustive `when` and a runtime `NoWhenBranchMatchedException` in a compiled one; Apollo's sealed hierarchy shows the cost.

asBuilt.summary: Built as decided in S2: `HttpFailure` with its two groups, `TransportFailure` with its eleven leaves and `UpstreamFailure`, and the `RefusalReason` and `ExhaustedReason` constants classes. In procedure P3 the consumer tests constructed every public leaf without the opt-in.
asBuilt.tests: L1 gating: the consumer classes construct every public leaf without the opt-in (procedure P3 step 3). The Level 2 classes of the leaves and the reasons come in S4, with the Tests row.
asBuilt.verified: Procedure P3, recorded in `final-implementation.md` §3 on 2026-10-25; not committed yet.

verdict.summary: `HttpFailure`, an abstract, subclass-gated `Exception`, with the groups `TransportFailure` and `UpstreamFailure` and final leaves nested in their group: `Closed`, `BudgetExhausted`, `DecodeFailure`, eleven transport leaves, `RateLimited` and `UpstreamError`. Every leaf a seam implementer or a decoder creates has a public constructor; `RateLimited`'s is `internal`. `RefusalReason` and `ExhaustedReason` are open constants classes, equal by name.
verdict.defense: Nesting keeps `Timeout`, `Protocol` and `Io` out of the flat package, where a top-level class would shadow a star-imported OkHttp or Okio name. Every message is a constant per type plus non-sensitive fields; `UpstreamError` copies its body in and out and never prints headers or body.

rows.name: Request and response types
rows.where: common/ — HttpMethod, Url, HttpHeaders, RequestBody, HttpRequest, HttpResponse, RedirectHop

gap.summary: No library-owned request or response type exists. `Connector` reads a URL line by line over `java.net.URLConnection` and offers one-shot helpers over Unirest, skrapeit and jsoup, so a URL, headers, a body and a response have no type of their own that a port could take.
evidence: webtools-scraping/src/main/kotlin/com/spartanlabs/webtools/scraping/Connector.kt:85 — `open(urlName: String)`, the line reader over `URLConnection` (baseline)
webtools-scraping/src/main/kotlin/com/spartanlabs/webtools/scraping/Connector.kt:263 — `get(url: String)`, the one-shot Unirest call (baseline)

options.name: Plain common classes: a validated `Url` parsed once, ordered case-insensitive `HttpHeaders` with per-entry sensitive flags, and `HttpRequest` and `HttpResponse` built by factory and builder, the response carrying its redirect chain as `RedirectHop(url, status)`
options.why: Vocabulary with no platform content compiles in common code, and a builder over an `internal` constructor is additive by construction. `Url` is `http` or `https` only, with no user-info and a query-free `redacted()`. Developer-written values are checked with `require`, and text from outside the process returns `Result`. No received-at time, which would bypass the injected clock, no charset and no streaming.

options.name: A JVM `actual typealias` to OkHttp's `HttpUrl` and `Headers`
options.why: It would put OkHttp in a public signature.

options.name: `java.net.URI` as the URL model
options.why: It parses hosts differently from OkHttp, the parser-disagreement bypass. The port's own `Url` is converted to `HttpUrl` inside the transport instead, and a differential test pins their agreement.

options.name: Flat constructors with defaulted parameters plus hidden deprecated overloads
options.why: A permanent overload per addition, kept correct by hand, and `@IntroducedAt` is Kotlin 2.3+; builders are additive by construction.

options.name: A public `Url` builder or `withQuery`, or building URLs with `HttpUrl.Builder`
options.why: Building a URL from parts is the facades' job, as text through the `internal` encoders and then `Url.parse`, so one parser and one canonical form decide the result; `HttpUrl.Builder` treats empty segments differently from text assembly. A public builder stays additive later.

options.name: Internationalised host names in `Url`
options.why: 1.0.0 refuses them, `xn--` labels included; supporting them needs an IDNA path that agrees with OkHttp's UTS 46 mapping.

options.name: Refusing transport-owned header names (`Host`, `Content-Length`, `User-Agent`, `Connection`, `Transfer-Encoding`) in `HttpRequest`
options.why: What the transport does with them is unit 6's to settle; the research left it open.

options.name: Kotlin's `lowercase()` and `equals(ignoreCase = true)` for header names, schemes and hosts
options.why: They fold U+212A (Kelvin) to `k` and U+0131 to `i`, so protocol text uses an ASCII-only fold written by hand.

The check module's `js` compile passed with the S3 files, so `Url` uses no JVM API.

verdict.summary: `HttpMethod`, `Url`, `HttpHeaders`, `RequestBody`, `HttpRequest`, `HttpResponse` and `RedirectHop`, with the shared predicates in `internal object HttpSyntax`. `Url.parse` reads like OkHttp 5.5.0's `HttpUrl` for ASCII hosts and is only ever stricter; `toString()` is the full canonical URL and `redacted()` the form for logs. Header names are RFC 9110 tokens, and `HttpRequest` refuses `CONNECT`, a body on `GET`, `HEAD` or `TRACE`, a value it cannot send and a second content type.
verdict.defense: Configurable types are built by a factory over an `internal` constructor, so later additions stay additive. Developer-written values throw `IllegalArgumentException`, and text from outside the process returns `Result` with a message that never echoes the input. Byte arrays are copied in and out, and the types print their structure only. The `Url` rules follow the user's two answers at the interview.

gap.summary: Nothing offers a suspend request. `Connector`, the only HTTP client, is blocking and stateful: it sets the JVM-wide `http.agent` on every connect and calls `Unirest.setTimeouts(0, 0)` in its `init`, and there is no port a consumer or a fake could substitute.

options.name: `HttpTransport : AutoCloseable`, a subclass-gated interface with one `suspend fun execute(request): Result<HttpResponse>` and a `close()` with an empty default body
options.why: Consumers and the fakes substitute it, and an interface is a narrower contract than an overridable class and gates cleanly. `./gradlew build` and `check` also run the module's compile, tests, `apiCheck` and `verifyJavaFloor` and the check module's `js` compile. A configuration-cache miss prints one more warning, "JS Environment Not Selected"; nothing downloads Node.js or Yarn, and the root project gains no plugin and no task.

They build on this vocabulary: the failure leaves and reasons, `Url`'s canonical host, the transport contract, `WallClock`, the logging seam and helpers, and the check-module pattern. Unit 6 holds the first top-level implementer of a gated port.

adaptation.summary: Its fixtures source sets opt in themselves for the fakes that implement `HttpTransport` and `WallClock`. The root project still has no `check` task, so where the publication check attaches stays its decision.
Nothing moves onto `webtools-http` before 1.0.0 is released: `Connector`, `WebViewer` and the legacy `ResultExtensions.kt` copies are unchanged.

api.summary: The one opt-in marker of the stack's seams, used only through `@SubclassOptInRequired` and `@OptIn`, and never removed.
Implementing either needs the opt-in. Calling and passing them are Stable Core, and `WallClock.System` is usable without opting in.
Subclassing a group needs the opt-in; matching the groups with an `else` does not.
Final leaves nested in their group, and two open constants classes that may gain constants in a feature release.
The request and response vocabulary, with factories over `internal` constructors and value or identity equality per type.
Internal helpers the later units of the module reuse; nothing a consumer reaches.

`webtools-udp` multiplatform: can reuse the check-module pattern and the logging seam.
